questions.stem: A 22-year-old client is admitted with suspected appendicitis. The nurse is sorting the admission findings into local signs at the appendix and signs that the inflammation has become systemic. Which findings indicate a systemic inflammatory response? Select all that apply.
options: Rebound tenderness at McBurney point
HR 104/min
Right hip held flexed while lying still
WBC 14,600/mm³ with 8% bands
RR 20/min
optionRationales: Rebound tenderness is a local sign: pain and tenderness over the inflamed organ itself.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign; mediators have reset the brain’s thermostat.
Correct. A heart rate above 90/min is one of the systemic cutoffs on the slides.
Holding the hip flexed is guarding, a local loss-of-function sign caused by pain at the site.
Correct. A WBC above 12,000/mm³ with increased bands shows the bone marrow is responding to the whole-body demand.
An RR of 20/min does not exceed the systemic cutoff of more than 20 breaths/min.
questions.rationale: The client has both kinds of findings. Rebound tenderness and a flexed, guarded hip are local cardinal signs (pain and loss of function) at the appendix. Fever above 38.5 °C, HR above 90, and WBC above 12,000 with bands meet the slide cutoffs for a systemic response, which means the inflammation is no longer contained. An RR of exactly 20 does not meet the cutoff of more than 20.
questions.takeaway: Local = signs at the organ (tenderness, guarding). Systemic = T >38.5 °C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12,000 or ↑ bands.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five cardinal signs seen at a site and the four systemic cutoffs from the assessment slide.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each finding: is it located at the appendix, or is it a whole-body measurement? Then compare each whole-body number with its exact cutoff.

questions.stem: A client with right lower quadrant pain has WBC 15,200/mm³, neutrophils 81%, and bands 12%. The client asks, “What does it mean that my ‘bands’ are high?” Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Your bone marrow is releasing young neutrophils early to fight a sudden bacterial process.”
“Your body is making allergy antibodies, which means you are reacting to a medication you took.”
“Your white cells are wearing out, so your immune system is too weak to fight infection.”
“Macrophages are laying down scar tissue, so the appendix inflammation is already healing.”
optionRationales: Correct. Bands are immature neutrophils. A rise (left shift) reflects the cellular response of acute inflammation, usually bacterial.
Bands are neutrophils, not IgE antibodies; a left shift does not indicate an allergic reaction.
A high WBC with bands shows a strong, active response, not a weak or suppressed immune system.
Scar formation belongs to the reparative stage and is not measured by bands; bands show an active acute response.
questions.rationale: In the cellular response of Stage 1, neutrophils are the first responders. When the demand is sudden, the bone marrow releases young neutrophils (bands) before they mature, creating a left shift. Neutrophil-driven responses with bands are typical of acute, usually bacterial, inflammation such as appendicitis, not chronic or allergic processes.
questions.takeaway: ↑ Bands = left shift = acute, neutrophil-driven (usually bacterial) inflammation.
questions.hintContent: Connect the white blood cell that arrives first in the cellular response with what an immature form of that cell in the blood means.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what type of cell a band is, then decide which type of inflammation (acute or chronic, bacterial or allergic) is driven by that cell.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with suspected appendicitis took ibuprofen 400 mg at home 2 hours ago “for the fever.” Findings now: T 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), HR 112/min, RR 24/min, WBC 16,000/mm³ with 12% bands, and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Which conclusion is most important for the nurse to communicate to the provider?
options: The inflammation is still local because the temperature is below 38.5 °C
The systemic response may be more severe than the temperature shows
The ibuprofen has treated the inflammation, so surgery may not be needed
The high bands suggest an allergic reaction to the ibuprofen taken at home
optionRationales: HR, RR, and WBC with bands all meet systemic cutoffs, so the process is not local even with a lower temperature.
Correct. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandins and lowers fever, so the measured temperature may understate a systemic response that the HR, RR, and WBC already show.
Ibuprofen reduces pain and fever by blocking prostaglandins; it does not remove the inflamed, infected appendix.
A left shift reflects an acute bacterial response, not an allergy to the drug.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs block prostaglandins, the mediators that reset the thermostat, so a recent dose can hide fever. The other systemic cutoffs are clearly met (HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12,000 with bands), and rebound tenderness is a worrying local sign. The key conclusion to report is that the inflammation is systemic and possibly worse than the temperature suggests.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs (and steroids) can mask fever; judge a systemic response by all the cutoffs, not the temperature alone.
questions.hintContent: Link how ibuprofen works on prostaglandins with the four systemic signs of inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each value against its systemic cutoff, then ask which finding a recent medication could be hiding.

questions.stem: A client with suspected appendicitis is awaiting CT results and reports right lower quadrant pain of 8/10. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the client NPO and explain the reason
Apply a heating pad to the right lower quadrant for comfort
Give the prescribed IV morphine for the severe pain
Give a PRN bisacodyl suppository for the lack of a bowel movement
Monitor temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate for rising values
Hold all pain medication so it does not mask worsening symptoms
optionRationales: Correct. NPO rests the inflamed bowel and prepares the client for possible surgery and anesthesia.
Heat causes vasodilation, bringing more blood to the inflamed appendix and increasing the risk of rupture.
Correct. Severe pain should be treated with the prescribed analgesic; current practice is to relieve pain while continuing to reassess.
Laxatives and suppositories increase pressure and movement in the bowel and can cause the appendix to rupture.
Correct. Rising temperature, HR, and RR signal a worsening systemic response or perforation.
Withholding analgesia “so it won’t mask symptoms” is outdated; pain should be managed while the nurse keeps reassessing.
questions.rationale: Care for an inflamed appendix combines resting the organ (NPO), pain control, and close watching for systemic spread. Heat is avoided because vasodilation increases blood flow and swelling at an already inflamed site, and laxatives raise pressure in the bowel; both can lead to perforation. Pain medication is given as prescribed rather than withheld.
questions.takeaway: Suspected appendicitis: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, monitor systemic signs; no heat, laxatives, or enemas.
questions.hintContent: Connect what heat does to blood vessels at an inflamed site with the risk of rupture, and recall the current approach to analgesia before surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask: does it rest and protect the inflamed organ, or does it add blood flow or pressure to it?

questions.stem: A client with appendicitis is awaiting surgery. The client says, “The pain suddenly got a lot better about 30 minutes ago, but now my whole belly hurts.” The abdomen is rigid and board-like. T 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), HR 124/min, RR 26/min, BP 96/58 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN IV morphine and reassess the pain in 30 minutes
Reassure the client that the relief means the swelling is going down
Give acetaminophen and apply cool cloths to lower the temperature
Notify the surgeon of the findings immediately using SBAR
optionRationales: Pain control matters, but treating the pain first delays the surgical team’s response to a likely perforation.
Sudden relief followed by diffuse pain suggests the appendix burst; false reassurance delays care.
The fever is a symptom of spreading infection; cooling measures do not address the cause.
Correct. Sudden relief, then diffuse pain, a rigid abdomen, and worsening systemic signs suggest perforation with peritonitis, which needs the surgeon now.
questions.rationale: Local appendix pain that suddenly eases and then spreads across a rigid abdomen means the inflamed appendix has likely perforated, spreading infection through the abdomen. The rising temperature, HR, and RR and the falling BP confirm the response is systemic and worsening. This cannot be managed by the nurse alone, so the surgeon is notified immediately.
questions.takeaway: Appendicitis + sudden relief then diffuse pain, rigid belly, and worsening vital signs = perforation; call the surgeon now.
questions.hintContent: Connect a change from localized to generalized abdominal pain with the trend of the systemic signs.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether this is an expected change or a new complication, then choose the action that gets definitive treatment fastest.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: On postoperative day 2 after surgery for a perforated appendix, a client’s temperature has fallen from 38.9 °C to 37.4 °C, WBC from 16,200 to 10,200/mm³ with 4% bands, and CRP is decreasing. The umbilical port site has redness extending 3 cm, is warm and firm, and has cloudy yellow drainage. Which action is the nurse’s priority?
options: Document that the client is improving because the systemic markers are falling
Report the port-site findings to the surgeon
Apply a warm compress to the port site and recheck it at the next shift
Advance the diet as ordered and reassess the incision tomorrow morning
optionRationales: Systemic markers can improve while a local wound infection begins; each finding must be judged separately.
Correct. Spreading redness, warmth, induration, and cloudy (purulent) drainage suggest a port-site infection that needs follow-up.
A warm compress does not treat a developing infection and delays reporting it.
Advancing the diet is appropriate, but waiting until tomorrow to reassess leaves a possible infection unreported.
questions.rationale: Falling temperature, WBC, bands, and CRP show the systemic response is resolving. But the incision tells a separate story: cloudy yellow drainage is purulent exudate, and spreading redness with warmth and induration means local infection. Improvement in one area does not cancel a new problem in another, so the nurse reports the wound findings.
questions.takeaway: Judge systemic markers and the wound separately; purulent drainage with spreading redness needs reporting even when labs improve.
questions.hintContent: Connect the types of exudate with what falling WBC and CRP can and cannot tell you.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate the whole-body trend from the local wound findings, then ask whether any single finding is abnormal on its own.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1815: 46-year-old client admitted yesterday with a leg abscess after incision and drainage. Allergy band states 'shellfish.' Family brought in a seafood pasta dish at 1750. Client now reports an itchy, swollen mouth and 'tightness in my throat.' Voice is hoarse. Raised, red wheals over chest, back, and arms. Reports crampy abdominal pain and has vomited once. Audible expiratory wheezes. Saline lock in left forearm is patent.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Anaphylaxis protocol: epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) IM; may repeat every 5–15 min
  • Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94%
  • 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus for SBP < 90 mm Hg
  • Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV once after epinephrine
  • Activate rapid response team

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses’ Notes, Vital Signs, and Orders. The rapid response team has been called. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give diphenhydramine 50 mg IV and reassess in 15 minutes
Apply oxygen by nonrebreather mask to raise the SpO₂
Give epinephrine 0.5 mg IM into the lateral thigh
Start the 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus
optionRationales: Diphenhydramine blocks only histamine, acts slowly, and does not open the airway or raise BP; the order specifies after epinephrine.
Oxygen is needed, but it does not reverse the airway swelling and vasodilation causing the low SpO₂.
Correct. Epinephrine constricts vessels and opens the airways, directly reversing the body-wide mediator release.
The bolus supports BP, but without epinephrine the vessels keep dilating and leaking.
questions.rationale: Skin (wheals), airway (hoarseness, throat tightness, wheezing), GI (cramps, vomiting), and circulation (BP 84/50, HR 124) are all involved after a known allergen. Massive mast-cell release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators is causing widespread vasodilation, capillary leak, and bronchoconstriction. Epinephrine is the only drug that reverses all of these, so it comes first; oxygen, fluids, and antihistamines are supportive.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM first. Antihistamines block one mediator and never replace epinephrine.
questions.hintContent: Connect which mediators are released in anaphylaxis with what each drug on the order sheet can and cannot reverse.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition from the systems involved, then pick the one intervention that treats the cause of both the airway and circulation problems.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The school nurse is called to the cafeteria for a 14-year-old with a known peanut allergy who ate a cookie containing peanuts 15 minutes ago. Which findings indicate that mediator release has become body-wide and the student needs epinephrine now? Select all that apply.
options: Hives spreading across the chest and neck
Repeated vomiting
Hoarse voice
HR 96/min and BP 110/68 mm Hg
History of seasonal allergies
Used an albuterol inhaler 3 days ago
optionRationales: Correct. Spreading hives show histamine acting on skin vessels beyond a local site.
Correct. Mediators acting on gut smooth muscle cause vomiting; skin plus GI after a known allergen already meets the two-system rule.
Correct. Hoarseness means capillary leak is swelling the larynx, an airway threat.
Near-normal vital signs do not rule out anaphylaxis; epinephrine should not wait for low BP.
Seasonal allergies are history, not a current sign of this reaction.
Past inhaler use is history and does not indicate the current reaction.
questions.rationale: Mast cells release histamine and other mediators that dilate and leak vessels (hives, laryngeal swelling) and act on smooth muscle (vomiting, wheezing). When two or more body systems are involved suddenly after a likely trigger, or any airway sign is present, it is anaphylaxis and epinephrine is given immediately. The student has skin, GI, and airway involvement; normal BP does not change that.
questions.takeaway: Two or more systems after a trigger, or any airway sign, = anaphylaxis. Do not wait for low BP.
questions.hintContent: Connect each mediator effect (vessel leak, smooth muscle contraction, itching) with the body system where you would see it.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep only current findings, then count how many body systems they involve.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone 10 mg daily for 9 months. Which statements by the client at a follow-up visit indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “I take my prednisone with breakfast every morning.”
“I skip it for a few days when my joints feel good.”
“I check my blood sugar when I feel extra thirsty.”
“I stopped my calcium and vitamin D because my bones feel fine.”
“A sore throat isn’t worth reporting unless I get a high fever.”
“I tell my dentist and other providers that I take a steroid.”
optionRationales: Taking prednisone in the morning with food matches the natural cortisol rhythm and protects the stomach; this is correct.
Correct. Skipping doses after long-term use can cause adrenal insufficiency; steroids must never be stopped suddenly.
Steroids raise blood glucose, so checking glucose when thirsty is appropriate.
Correct. Steroids cause bone loss silently; calcium and vitamin D are needed even when the client feels fine.
Correct. Steroids blunt fever and redness, so a sore throat may be the only early sign of infection and should be reported.
Telling every provider about steroid use is correct.
questions.rationale: Long-term prednisone suppresses the adrenal glands, raises glucose, thins bone, and suppresses the inflammatory response. Because the classic signs and fever are blunted, a client on steroids cannot wait for a high fever before reporting possible infection. Skipping doses and stopping bone protection also show the teaching was not understood.
questions.takeaway: Steroids: never skip or stop suddenly, protect bone, watch glucose, and report small signs of infection because fever is masked.
questions.hintContent: Link the adverse effects of long-term corticosteroids with how steroids change the assessment of infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Read each statement as a behavior and ask whether it protects the client from a known steroid risk or exposes them to one.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client from an assisted-living facility is admitted with a productive cough. Baseline: alert and oriented ×3, walks with a walker. Which findings should the nurse recognize as cues of a worsening infection with a systemic response? Select all that apply.
options: New confusion since yesterday
Temperature 35.8 °C (96.4 °F)
HR 102/min
RR 18/min
BP 132/78 mm Hg
WBC 13,800/mm³
optionRationales: Correct. In older adults, new confusion is often the first sign of infection and is a change from this client’s baseline.
Correct. A temperature below 36 °C is a systemic sign on the slides; older adults often run low instead of febrile.
Correct. A heart rate above 90/min meets the systemic cutoff.
An RR of 18/min is within normal limits and does not meet the cutoff of more than 20.
This BP is within an acceptable range and is not a systemic sign.
Correct. A WBC above 12,000/mm³ meets the systemic cutoff.
questions.rationale: Older adults often have a blunted fever response, so infection may show up as a low temperature or as new confusion compared with baseline. The low temperature, HR above 90, and WBC above 12,000 meet the slide cutoffs for systemic inflammation, and the new confusion is the typical atypical presentation of infection in this age group.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, a LOW temperature and new confusion can signal infection; compare with the client’s own baseline.
questions.hintContent: Combine the systemic cutoffs (including the low-temperature cutoff) with how infection presents in older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each vital sign and lab against its cutoff in both directions, then compare the behavior finding with the stated baseline.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: During a preoperative interview for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a client states, “The last time a dentist wore rubber gloves, I broke out in hives and my lips swelled.” Which action is the nurse’s priority?
options: Notify the surgical team and arrange a latex-safe environment
Document the reaction in the chart as a minor skin sensitivity
Ask the provider to prescribe an antihistamine before the surgery
Explain that a skin reaction to gloves will not affect the surgery
optionRationales: Correct. Latex is an anaphylaxis trigger, and lip swelling shows more than a skin reaction; the perioperative team must avoid latex exposure.
Lip swelling is not minor; documenting it as a skin sensitivity underestimates the risk.
An antihistamine does not prevent anaphylaxis; avoiding the trigger does.
Surgery involves many latex products, so this reassurance is false and unsafe.
questions.rationale: Latex is one of the four anaphylaxis trigger groups on the slides, and lip swelling indicates a significant reaction. The nurse’s preoperative role includes identifying risks and communicating them so the surgical team can prepare a latex-safe environment. Prevention means avoiding the trigger.
questions.takeaway: A latex reaction with lip swelling before surgery = notify the team and set up latex-safe care.
questions.hintContent: Connect the slide list of anaphylaxis triggers with the nurse’s role in preoperative care.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide how serious the reported reaction was, then choose the action that prevents re-exposure.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 7-year-old who weighs 24 kg (53 lb) and has a tree-nut allergy how to use a 0.15-mg epinephrine auto-injector. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I can inject it into the outer thigh even through his jeans.”
“After I give the injection, I will call 911 even if he seems better.”
“His dose is smaller than an adult’s dose because it is based on his body weight.”
“If he has hives and keeps vomiting, I’ll give an antihistamine and wait.”
optionRationales: The outer thigh is the correct site, and the auto-injector can be given through clothing.
Symptoms can return, so calling 911 after every use is correct.
Children’s doses are weight-based; this shows correct understanding.
Correct. Skin plus GI symptoms after the allergen is anaphylaxis; an antihistamine cannot replace epinephrine, and waiting delays life-saving care.
questions.rationale: Two body systems (skin and GI) involved after a known allergen meet the definition of anaphylaxis, so epinephrine is given right away. Antihistamines block only histamine and act slowly. The parent correctly understands the injection site, calling 911, and weight-based pediatric dosing.
questions.takeaway: Hives + vomiting after a known allergen = epinephrine now, then 911. Pediatric doses are weight-based.
questions.hintContent: Connect the two-system rule for anaphylaxis with why an antihistamine is not first-line, and recall how children’s doses are chosen.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the statement that would delay the first-line drug.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An off-duty nurse at a community picnic sees an adult who was just stung by a bee. The adult has facial swelling, wheezing, and dizziness and is carrying an epinephrine auto-injector. The nurse has directed a bystander to call 911 and has checked the adult’s breathing. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Help the adult walk to a shaded area to sit down
Give the adult an oral antihistamine from the first-aid kit
Administer the auto-injector into the adult’s outer thigh
Note the time and watch for improvement for 5 to 15 minutes
optionRationales: A dizzy person with possible hypotension should not stand or walk; sudden standing can cause collapse.
An oral antihistamine is slow and does not open the airway or raise BP.
Correct. Once EMS is called, epinephrine IM into the outer thigh is the priority.
Timing and monitoring come after epinephrine is given, not instead of it.
questions.rationale: Outside the hospital the slide treatment is immediate epinephrine plus EMS activation. EMS has been called, so the next action is the auto-injector into the outer thigh. Then the person lies down with legs raised, the time is noted, and a second dose is given if symptoms continue.
questions.takeaway: Community anaphylaxis: call 911, epinephrine auto-injector into the outer thigh, then position and monitor.
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide treatment for anaphylaxis outside the hospital.
questions.hintStrategy: Note which steps are already done, then choose the next step in the sequence.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit receives four client updates at the same time. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports 90 minutes of morning stiffness in both hands today
A client with cellulitis who has a temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) on day 1 of IV antibiotics
A client taking prednisone 40 mg daily whose fasting blood glucose this morning is 168 mg/dL
A client with a peanut allergy who has an itchy throat and a hoarse voice after a visitor’s snack
optionRationales: Prolonged morning stiffness is an expected symptom of chronic RA and is stable.
A temperature of 38.0 °C is below the systemic cutoff of 38.5 °C and is not unexpected on day 1 of antibiotics.
Hyperglycemia is an expected steroid adverse effect that needs follow-up but is not immediately life-threatening.
Correct. Hoarseness after allergen exposure signals laryngeal swelling from anaphylaxis, an airway emergency.
questions.rationale: Use the ABCs, then unstable before stable. Hoarseness and throat symptoms after a known allergen mean the airway is swelling. The RA stiffness is a chronic, expected finding; the cellulitis temperature does not yet meet the systemic cutoff early in treatment; and steroid-induced hyperglycemia is an expected adverse effect that can be addressed after the airway threat.
questions.takeaway: Airway threat from anaphylaxis beats chronic, expected, and medication-related findings.
questions.hintContent: Weigh an airway sign after an allergen against a chronic symptom, a borderline temperature, and a known steroid effect.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the ABCs first, then ask which findings are expected for the condition or drug.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: An adult client is being discharged after treatment for anaphylaxis caused by shellfish. Which instructions should the nurse include in the discharge teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Carry two epinephrine auto-injectors at all times
Keep the auto-injector in the car’s glove compartment
Wear a medical alert bracelet that identifies the allergy
Take an antihistamine first and use epinephrine only if it fails
Read food labels and ask about shellfish in restaurant dishes
Schedule a follow-up appointment with an allergist
optionRationales: Correct. A second dose may be needed if symptoms continue or return.
Heat in a car can damage epinephrine, and the drug must be with the client wherever a reaction could happen.
Correct. A medical alert ID informs responders if the client cannot speak.
Antihistamines never replace epinephrine; delaying epinephrine is a leading cause of death in anaphylaxis.
Correct. Prevention means avoiding the trigger.
Correct. Allergist follow-up supports testing and long-term planning.
questions.rationale: Prevention on the slides means avoiding triggers, so the client learns to read labels and ask about ingredients. Because epinephrine is the only first-line drug, the client carries two auto-injectors at room temperature and never substitutes an antihistamine. A medical ID and allergist follow-up complete the plan.
questions.takeaway: Avoid the trigger, carry two auto-injectors on your body, wear medical ID, and see an allergist; antihistamines never come first.
questions.hintContent: Combine prevention (trigger avoidance) with what you know about epinephrine versus antihistamines.
questions.hintStrategy: Accept options that prevent exposure or speed epinephrine; reject any that delay or damage it.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is on day 5 of IV antibiotics for an infected leg wound. The CRP has decreased from 12.4 mg/dL to 3.1 mg/dL, and the ESR from 72 mm/hr to 68 mm/hr. The wound drainage has changed from thick yellow-green to scant and serous. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?
options: The antibiotics are failing because the ESR is still high
The lab values conflict, so a laboratory error is likely
Treatment is working; the ESR falls more slowly than CRP
The thinner drainage shows a new infection is developing
optionRationales: ESR rises and falls slowly and can stay high for weeks after improvement, so it does not show treatment failure.
CRP and ESR normally change at different speeds; this pattern is expected, not an error.
Correct. The falling CRP and the change from purulent to serous drainage both show the infection is responding.
A change from purulent to scant serous drainage is a healthy trend, not a sign of new infection.
questions.rationale: CRP rises and falls quickly, which makes it the better marker for monitoring treatment, while ESR lags. The wound confirms the lab trend: purulent exudate (dead neutrophils and bacteria) has given way to scant serous exudate, which is seen late in healing. Both pieces of data point to an effective response.
questions.takeaway: Falling CRP + drainage changing from purulent to serous = treatment working, even if ESR is still high.
questions.hintContent: Connect how quickly CRP and ESR change with what each type of wound exudate means.
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the fast marker, the slow marker, and the wound trend separately, then see if they agree.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client on postoperative day 2 after an open colectomy for ulcerative colitis. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Pink edges extending 2 mm from the approximated incision
Scant serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
Red streak extending 5 cm from the incision toward the flank
Thick, cloudy drainage with a foul odor
Mild tenderness around the incision
optionRationales: A narrow pink border along a closed incision is expected inflammation during healing.
Scant serosanguineous drainage is expected in the first days after surgery.
Correct. A red streak moving away from the wound means inflammation or infection is spreading.
Correct. Thick, cloudy, foul-smelling drainage is purulent exudate and suggests wound infection.
Mild tenderness is an expected local sign early after surgery.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C with HR above 90 meets the systemic cutoffs.
questions.rationale: Every incision causes some inflammation: narrow pink edges, mild tenderness, and scant serosanguineous drainage are expected. Findings that need follow-up are spreading redness (a red streak), purulent exudate, and systemic signs (fever above 38.5 °C and tachycardia), which show the process is no longer contained and healing is off track.
questions.takeaway: Expected incision: narrow pink edges, mild tenderness, scant pink drainage. Report streaks, pus, and systemic signs.
questions.hintContent: Connect the drainage types, expected local inflammation after surgery, and the systemic cutoffs.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding as expected healing, spreading local problem, or systemic sign.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with joint pain, fatigue, and a rash across the cheeks is being evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Her ESR is 58 mm/hr. Which finding on serum protein electrophoresis should the nurse expect if SLE is confirmed?
options: Decreased gamma globulin with increased albumin
Increased gamma globulin with decreased albumin
Normal protein fractions with a normal albumin
Decreased gamma globulin with decreased albumin
optionRationales: SLE involves overproduction of antibodies, so gamma globulin rises rather than falls.
Correct. In SLE the immune system overproduces antibodies (gamma globulins), and albumin often falls with chronic inflammation.
An active autoimmune process with an ESR of 58 (normal for women 0–20) is not expected to show normal fractions.
Gamma globulin is increased, not decreased, in SLE.
questions.rationale: SLE is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. The ESR of 58 mm/hr is well above the female range of 0–20, showing active inflammation. The slides list increased gamma globulin (antibodies) and decreased albumin on protein electrophoresis in SLE.
questions.takeaway: SLE: ↑ ESR, ↑ gamma globulin, ↓ albumin.
questions.hintContent: Connect SLE as an autoimmune (chronic) inflammatory disease with what gamma globulins are.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether the immune system is overproducing or underproducing antibodies in autoimmune disease.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning results for four clients. Which client’s results should the nurse report to the provider first?
options: An 80-year-old with pneumonia: T 35.7 °C (96.3 °F), HR 118, RR 28, WBC 14,800/mm³ with 18% bands
A client with rheumatoid arthritis whose ESR is 24 mm/hr, down from 40 mm/hr last month
A client with a healing leg wound whose WBC fell from 13,000/mm³ to 9,400/mm³
A client with lupus whose serum protein electrophoresis shows increased gamma globulin and decreased albumin
optionRationales: Correct. A temperature below 36 °C, HR above 90, RR above 20, and WBC above 12,000 with bands meet every systemic cutoff; older adults often run low rather than febrile.
A falling ESR in chronic RA shows improving inflammation.
A WBC returning to normal shows the wound infection is resolving.
These are expected findings in SLE, a known chronic condition.
questions.rationale: Systemic beats local and unstable beats stable. The older adult with pneumonia meets every slide cutoff for a systemic response, including a low temperature, which is a common presentation at this age. The other results show improving acute or chronic inflammation or findings expected for a known diagnosis.
questions.takeaway: A LOW temperature with tachycardia, tachypnea, and a left shift in an older adult is a systemic response; report it first.
questions.hintContent: Combine the systemic cutoffs (including low temperature) with how older adults present with infection and how chronic disease markers trend.
questions.hintStrategy: Mark each client as improving, expected, or unstable, then report the unstable one.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client has taken high-dose aspirin for arthritis pain and recently started another over-the-counter product that also contains aspirin. The client’s daughter says, “Mom’s confusion is probably just her age.” Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of salicylate toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Pinpoint pupils
New confusion
Nausea and vomiting
Heart rate of 48/min
optionRationales: Correct. Tinnitus is an early sign of salicylate toxicity.
Correct. Hyperventilation (rapid, deep breathing) is a sign of salicylate toxicity.
Pinpoint pupils suggest opioid effect, not salicylate toxicity.
Correct. Confusion is a sign of toxicity; a new change in an older adult should not be dismissed as aging.
Correct. Nausea and vomiting occur with salicylate toxicity.
Bradycardia is not a sign of salicylate toxicity.
questions.rationale: Toxicity often occurs when high-dose aspirin is combined with another OTC product that also contains aspirin. Signs include tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea and vomiting, rapid deep breathing, and confusion. In older adults, new confusion is a change from baseline that needs to be investigated, not attributed to age.
questions.takeaway: Tinnitus + hyperventilation + N/V + confusion on aspirin = salicylate toxicity; new confusion in an older adult is never “just age.”
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs of salicylate toxicity and how new confusion should be interpreted in an older adult.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep findings that match aspirin excess; reject those typical of other drugs.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with acute elbow bursitis has been taking ibuprofen and asks, “Can I switch to acetaminophen? My neighbor says it works the same on the swelling.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Acetaminophen blocks histamine, so it reduces the swelling just as well.”
“Both drugs block prostaglandins equally, so either will shrink the swelling.”
“Acetaminophen is also an NSAID, so it has the same benefits and risks.”
“Acetaminophen eases pain and fever but does little for the swelling.”
optionRationales: Acetaminophen does not block histamine, and blocking histamine is not how swelling from bursitis is treated.
Acetaminophen has very little anti-inflammatory effect at the site, unlike ibuprofen.
Acetaminophen is a non-opioid analgesic, not an NSAID; it spares the stomach but can harm the liver.
Correct. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory effect, so it will not reduce swelling.
questions.rationale: Swelling comes from increased capillary permeability driven by mediators such as prostaglandins. Ibuprofen, an NSAID, lowers prostaglandin production and so reduces pain, fever, and swelling. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has very little anti-inflammatory effect, so it will not bring the swelling down.
questions.takeaway: Acetaminophen = pain and fever only. NSAIDs = pain, fever, AND inflammation (swelling).
questions.hintContent: Connect which mediator causes the swelling with which drug class actually reduces it at the site.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what causes the swelling, then check which drug acts on that cause.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client is prescribed ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours for acute tendinitis. Which item in the client’s medication history is most important for the nurse to clarify with the prescriber before giving the first dose?
options: Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily
Loratadine 10 mg daily in spring
Warfarin 5 mg daily
Vitamin D 1,000 units daily
optionRationales: Levothyroxine has no important interaction with a short course of ibuprofen.
Loratadine, an antihistamine, does not raise the risk of NSAID harm.
Correct. An NSAID plus an anticoagulant greatly increases the risk of serious bleeding.
Vitamin D does not interact with ibuprofen.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs block prostaglandins everywhere, including those that protect the stomach lining and help platelets function. Combined with warfarin, the risk of serious GI and other bleeding rises sharply, so the prescription should be clarified before the first dose.
questions.takeaway: Question an NSAID in a client taking an anticoagulant.
questions.hintContent: Recall the adverse effects of NSAIDs and which other drugs add to them.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the medication whose risk overlaps with a known NSAID adverse effect.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing prescriptions for an oral NSAID written for several clients. For which clients should the nurse question the prescription? Select all that apply.
options: A 25-year-old with an ankle sprain and no medical history
A client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation
A client with chronic kidney disease and an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m²
A 32-year-old with primary dysmenorrhea
A client with a bleeding duodenal ulcer diagnosed last week
An 82-year-old who is dehydrated after 2 days of vomiting
optionRationales: An acute sprain in a healthy young adult is an appropriate use of an NSAID.
Correct. NSAIDs plus an anticoagulant greatly increase bleeding risk.
Correct. Prostaglandins help maintain kidney blood flow; blocking them can worsen advanced kidney disease.
Menstrual cramps are prostaglandin-driven pain and an appropriate use of an NSAID.
Correct. Blocking the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining worsens ulcers and bleeding.
Correct. In an older, dehydrated client, blocking prostaglandins further reduces kidney blood flow and raises the risk of kidney injury.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins cause pain and swelling, but they also protect the stomach lining, maintain kidney blood flow, and support platelet function. Blocking them explains why NSAIDs are questioned with anticoagulants, advanced kidney disease, active ulcers, and in older or dehydrated clients whose kidneys depend on prostaglandins to stay perfused.
questions.takeaway: Question NSAIDs with anticoagulants, kidney disease, GI bleeding or ulcers, and in older dehydrated clients.
questions.hintContent: Connect the protective jobs of prostaglandins with age- and volume-related kidney risk.
questions.hintStrategy: For each client, ask which protective prostaglandin job the NSAID would take away and whether that client depends on it.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who takes prednisone 30 mg daily for Crohn’s disease is on postoperative day 4 after a bowel resection. The client reports increasing incisional pain. T 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), HR 98/min, and the incision has slight swelling without redness. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: The findings are within expected limits for postoperative day 4
The prednisone may be masking signs of a developing infection
The prednisone has fully controlled the inflammation at the incision
Slight swelling without redness rules out a wound infection
optionRationales: Pain that increases on day 4 instead of easing, with a rising HR, is not the expected healing pattern.
Correct. Steroids suppress the inflammatory response, blunting fever and redness, so increasing pain and HR may be the only early clues.
Suppressing the classic signs does not mean the tissue is healing or free of infection.
Steroids can hide redness, so its absence does not rule out infection.
questions.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress the inflammatory response, so the cardinal signs (redness, heat, swelling) and fever that normally reveal infection are blunted. In a client on prednisone, subtle changes such as pain that increases instead of easing and a heart rate above 90 matter more and should be reported.
questions.takeaway: Steroids hide the classic signs; in these clients, rising pain or HR may be the only early sign of infection.
questions.hintContent: Connect how corticosteroids affect the cardinal signs with which assessment findings still change during infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask what you would normally expect to see with a wound infection and how the medication changes that picture.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis reports stiffness in the hands lasting about an hour each morning. There is no redness or warmth over the joints today. Which intervention should the nurse suggest?
options: Take a warm shower or soak the hands in warm water after waking
Apply ice packs to both hands for 60 minutes right after waking
Keep both hands immobilized in resting splints all day long
Delay all hand activity until the afternoon when stiffness eases
optionRationales: Correct. Heat causes vasodilation and relaxes stiff joints; it is appropriate for chronic stiffness without acute signs.
Cold is for acute swelling in the first 24–48 hours, and 60 minutes exceeds the safe 15–20 minute limit.
Constant immobilization worsens stiffness and loss of function in chronic arthritis.
Avoiding activity reduces mobility; gentle activity after warmth is preferred.
questions.rationale: RA is chronic inflammation. With no acute cardinal signs (redness, warmth) present, the problem is stiffness, not fresh swelling. Heat increases blood flow and relaxes stiff joints, so it is the right choice here, whereas cold is reserved for new, acutely swollen injuries.
questions.takeaway: Ice for fresh acute swelling; heat for chronic stiffness without acute redness or warmth.
questions.hintContent: Connect the difference between acute and chronic inflammation with the vessel effects of heat and cold.
questions.hintStrategy: Check whether acute cardinal signs are present, then match the therapy to the problem.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client admitted with acute cholecystitis is NPO and awaiting cholecystectomy. The client says, “I’m starving. Why can’t I just have a little something to eat?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “You need to stay NPO so the bowel shows clearly on tomorrow’s x-ray.”
“Food in your stomach would neutralize the antibiotics you are receiving through the IV.”
“Not eating will help you lose weight, which is important before surgery.”
“Eating makes your gallbladder contract, which worsens inflammation and pain.”
optionRationales: NPO in cholecystitis is not ordered to improve an x-ray image.
Food does not neutralize IV antibiotics.
Weight loss is not the purpose of preoperative NPO status.
Correct. Food triggers gallbladder contraction, increasing pain and inflammation; NPO rests the organ and prepares for anesthesia.
questions.rationale: When food arrives, a hormone signals the gallbladder to contract. In cholecystitis this increases pain and inflammation. Keeping the client NPO rests the inflamed organ and also prepares the client for anesthesia and surgery.
questions.takeaway: Cholecystitis: NPO rests the gallbladder (and prepares for surgery).
questions.hintContent: Recall what eating does to the gallbladder and why an inflamed organ is rested before surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that links eating to the inflamed organ itself.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 14-month-old who weighs 10 kg (22 lb) has had acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea for 2 days. The parent reports only two wet diapers today. The child is alert, with moist mucous membranes. Which intervention is the nurse’s priority?
options: Offer undiluted apple juice to replace the lost fluids
Give an over-the-counter antidiarrheal medication
Give small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution
Withhold all fluids for 24 hours to rest the bowel
optionRationales: Undiluted juice is high in sugar and can worsen diarrhea.
OTC antidiarrheals are not a nursing priority for a toddler and do not replace fluid.
Correct. Small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution replace fluid safely in mild to moderate dehydration; wet diapers then show whether it works.
Withholding fluids is dangerous for a toddler with a small total fluid volume.
questions.rationale: A toddler’s smaller total fluid volume and immature kidneys make fluid losses from GI inflammation more significant than in an adult. With the child still alert and mucous membranes moist, small, frequent oral rehydration solution is the priority, and the nurse evaluates by counting wet diapers rather than waiting for vital signs to change.
questions.takeaway: Children lose fluid faster: small, frequent ORS, and track wet diapers.
questions.hintContent: Connect a child’s fluid volume and kidney function with safe fluid replacement.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge how dehydrated the child is now, then pick the safest way to replace fluid for that level.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 15-year-old with Crohn’s disease has been taking prednisone for 6 weeks and tells the nurse, “I’m going to stop taking it. My face is so round and I have acne. Everyone at school stares at me.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Your health matters more than how you look, so keep taking it.”
“Tell me more about how these changes are affecting you at school.”
“Lots of teenagers have acne at your age, so nobody at school will really notice yours.”
“You can stop the prednisone once your symptoms are better.”
optionRationales: This dismisses the teen’s concern and makes it less likely the teen will keep taking the drug.
Correct. Exploring the body-image concern first builds trust; the nurse can then explain why the drug must not be stopped suddenly.
False reassurance minimizes the concern and closes the conversation.
Stopping prednisone suddenly after weeks of use risks adrenal insufficiency; it must be tapered.
questions.rationale: A round face and acne are expected steroid effects, and adolescents are especially sensitive to body image. Teens are more likely to keep taking a medication when they feel heard, so the nurse first explores the concern and then teaches that prednisone must never be stopped suddenly and that the provider can discuss options.
questions.takeaway: Teen upset about steroid effects: explore the concern first, then teach never to stop suddenly.
questions.hintContent: Combine adolescent developmental needs with the risks of stopping corticosteroids abruptly.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the therapeutic response that opens the conversation and does not give unsafe advice.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and frailty has a persistently elevated CRP with no acute illness. Which collaborative interventions should the nurse anticipate to reduce the client’s chronic inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Physical therapy referral for a progressive resistance training program
Bed rest to conserve the client’s energy
Dietitian referral for a plan rich in vegetables, fish, and whole grains
Daily high-dose NSAIDs to lower the CRP level
Support for improved control of blood glucose
A high-saturated-fat diet to prevent muscle loss
optionRationales: Correct. The slides state that inflammatory markers in older adults can be improved with resistance training.
Bed rest worsens frailty and muscle loss.
Correct. An anti-inflammatory diet guided by a dietitian lowers inflammation.
Long-term high-dose NSAIDs carry GI, kidney, and bleeding risks in older adults and are not the recommended approach.
Correct. Controlling diabetes is a modifiable factor that reduces chronic inflammation.
Saturated fat promotes inflammation; the dietitian aims to reduce it.
questions.rationale: CRP, a liver protein that rises with inflammation, is commonly higher in older adults, especially frail ones, and is linked to more illness and hospitalization. The slides say diet and resistance training improve these markers, and control of diabetes is a modifiable risk factor. The team approach uses a dietitian and physical therapist rather than drugs.
questions.takeaway: Frail older adult with high CRP: anti-inflammatory diet, resistance training, and glucose control.
questions.hintContent: Connect what an elevated CRP means with the lifespan slide on older adults and the collaborative team.
questions.hintStrategy: Accept options that change modifiable factors safely; reject those that add risk or inactivity.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with acute cellulitis of the forearm has received IV antibiotics for 48 hours. On admission, the nurse outlined the redness with a skin marker. Which finding best indicates that treatment is effective?
options: Redness has receded inside the marked border
Temperature has risen from 37.8 °C to 38.4 °C
Redness now extends 2 cm past the marked border
A new soft, fluid-filled area formed in the center
optionRationales: Correct. Shrinking redness inside the marked line shows the acute inflammation is resolving as the cause is treated.
A rising temperature suggests the process is worsening, not resolving.
Redness spreading past the border means the infection is spreading.
A new fluctuant area suggests abscess formation and needs to be reported.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation resolves once its cause is neutralized, so cellulitis should improve with antibiotics. Marking the border of redness gives an objective way to evaluate: redness inside the line means improvement, while spreading redness, a rising temperature, or a fluctuant area means the treatment is not working.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate cellulitis objectively: redness shrinking inside the marked border = treatment working.
questions.hintContent: Connect how acute inflammation behaves once the cause is treated with how the nurse measures redness over time.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the finding that shows the local process getting smaller, not larger.
